utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Just a very small matter. It relates to the development last night about the understanding that it is the Guards Motorised Brigade as opposed to OG South and Mr. Lukic saying that that matter had been put to the witnesses. We have examined all the transcripts that we believe are relevant. It has never ever been put to any witness directly. There have been elliptical questions in respect to Trifunovic. It was not put in the 65 ter; it has not been put in the summaries. There is nothing now that we can do with it, but I just wanted to make absolutely certain, so it was clear, that that was the facts as opposed to, perhaps, a misunderstanding by Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. May I remind you of the affirmation, Mr. Sljivancanin, that you made at the beginning of your evidence which still applies. The indications are that Mr. Sljivancanin did not hear what I have just said. Is the interpretation functioning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's functioning. I've just heard it now. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I shall respond to Mr. Moore straight away, and during the break I will find the page, that we asked the witness Trifunovic about Operations Group South, whether it was something that existed in actual fact or whether it was - how shall I put this? - a category that just existed on paper. I will find the page reference. I know the question was put. I even know what the answer was. On the other hand, in our first summary that we submitted according to Rule 65 ter, we decidedly say that Mr. Sljivancanin was the chief of security of the Guards Motorised Brigade and that is what we say in that summary; we also say what his job was as chief of security of the Guards Motorised Brigade. That can be seen in the first summary. Now I'm going to put a question to Mr. Sljivancanin about that. Before that, may I say that I agreed with Mr. Moore on this. Yesterday, they gave us another document that they intend to use in Mr. Sljivancanin's cross-examination or perhaps not, but then I asked that they give Mr. Sljivancanin a copy of that person's statement in B/C/S. We did receive this through disclosure. This is a statement made by a particular person before a military court in Belgrade, but I'm not sure that Mr. Sljivancanin has it. And I'm sure it's no problem to submit that to him during the break so that he would have his own copy in B/C/S. And now I shall go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, you know what the subject is and you know what was raised yesterday. What is Operations Group South? Where were you chief of security? Were you a member of the command of Operations Group South? And who comprised the command of Operations Group South?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning to all. Your Honours, perhaps it's going to be a bit of a lengthy answer, but I really wish to clarify this matter to show you what the truth is in this regard. I took the stand in order to say what I know and what is true. And now whether that suits someone or not, it is for you to judge. The Court has the power in its hands and my head can fly. That doesn't matter, but what matters is that I will tell the truth. I know that when I came to the area of Negoslavci, that there was a command that, at that time, introduced itself as the command of Operations Group South. I remember that in that command there were a few officers. I know two or three of their names for sure. The commander who introduced himself then was Colonel Rajo Bojat, and the Chief of Staff was also a colonel, Ljubicic, but I've forgotten his first name. I think that in that command there was an assistant for morale, Jelic Blagoje. I think he was a lieutenant colonel. And on the staff there were a few other officers and in their command as well, but I do not remember. A few days later, when the fighting started for deblocking the barracks and disarming the paramilitary formations, all of a sudden this command disappeared, if I can put it that way, and I know that Colonel Mrksic took over command over the units. What I knew then is that no one ever gave me an order or a paper, and if anyone has a paper of that kind, they can show it to me and I will apologise for everything I've been saying. I have only been appointed chief of security of the Guards Motorised Brigade and nothing else. There were organs that gave me professional guidance and that is the chief of security of the cabinet of the Federal Secretary, and apart from them, I did not ever receive any kind of specialist direction or instructions that I shall report to any other security organ in order to get any kind of direction with regard to counter-intelligence work. Anyone who has any such document can feel free to show it to me, but I don't think any such thing ever existed. While carrying out my tasks, I was never called by the security organs of the 1st Military District to any meeting, and I did not receive from them any document that had to do with counter-intelligence work in the zone. All the documents that I wish to show here and that I have and that have to do with counter-intelligence work and that came to me through security channels were addressed to the security organ of the Guards Motorised Brigade. All my documents that I sent, I sent as chief of security of the Guards Motorised Brigade. The next thing I wish to add with regard to this question: I'm not saying that I am that smart. I did go to military schools. There are military experts here. There are rules and regulations, according to which one worked then, in the units of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army. I observed these rules and I did my best to act in accordance with them. In the rules it says that operations groups can be set up as temporary units in order to carry out a temporary assignment that can last for one day, two days, three days, five days, and that operations -- and that an operations group consists of operations units. If we analyse this here, this so-called Operations Group South, namely, that it consisted of up to two brigades, then an assessment can be made as to whether this is an operations group or whatever else. I don't know what to call it. One more thing, Your Honours. Studying military regulations, I studied in military schools that units of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army were established on the basis of assessing territory of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, its strategic operations and tactical directions for use in conditions of war. If one looks at the map - and we can display a map here - if you look at Sid-Vukovar, that direction, as far as what I learned and what I knew, that direction can only be at a tactical level, the capacity of one reinforced brigade or perhaps simply one brigade. That is the next thing that I wish to corroborate that with. Further on, if we precisely analyse the documents that were presented by Commander Mrksic, will you see that in the order and decisions, he gave assignments to battalions, battalions from the Guards Motorised Brigade, that were the only ones that took part in deblocking the Vukovar barracks, and they acted in concert with the Territorial Defence of Vukovar. Other units were temporarily staying in this territory and they were being replaced and they were outside the town of Vukovar where there was no combat action. I, as chief of security of the Guards Motorised Brigade at that time, did everything I could in order to be in Vukovar with the soldiers of the Guards Motorised Brigade and to try to contribute to saving their lives and accomplishing this mission. That is what I wished to say. There are quite a few clever people here who can assess what is true and what is not true. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, let us clarify this a bit more. Out of many documents that were exhibited here and that we have discussed and shall discuss, a term is used, "Command of the Operations Group South" in the documents; that is the term used. I would like to ask you the following: Did you attend meetings? Actually I thought that I should ask you about this later, that we should discuss this later, but I believe that this is the right time to clarify this point. Were you part of this command? Did you attend these meetings? How often were these meetings held, and what was the content of these meetings?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, as for the term "Operations Group South," I accepted this as it was suggested to me that this should be a secret name so that formation names would not be mentioned, especially not the actual name of the Guards Brigade. I attended meetings that were held by Commander Mrksic and I remember that these meetings were certainly attended by all assistant commanders from the command of the Guards Brigade, in terms of establishment; then commanders at battalion and division level from the Guards Motorised Brigade; the commander of the Territorial Defence of Vukovar. And some meetings, depending on the presence of each and every unit in this territory, some meetings were attended by the commanders of brigades, either the Podinavska Brigade or the 80th or the 20th Partisan Brigade, depending on who was there when. As for battalion commanders from those brigades, they did not attend the meetings that I attended. When you ask me about these meetings and when they were held, they were held when the commander convened them; usually at nightfall, not every day, but when necessary. Sometimes they were held evening in the morning, say, at 7.00, at 8.00. All of that is recorded in the war log. And also there was a book recording these meetings that was kept by the Chief of Staff, and you can see it there, except that the commander, in accordance with his own ideas and necessity, he convened only meetings of some commanders sometimes, because if he thought that some commander needed additional guidance, then he would have such meetings. And that is what the war log says.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did these meetings evolve?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for how the meetings evolved, well, usually there was a plan for meetings, and, as far as I can remember, this is the way it went: First, subordinate commanders would report in accordance with an order set up by the Chief of Staff about assignments carried out and their tasks. Then, members of the command, or rather, the assistant commanders presented their views on what was going on in the units and they were responding in terms of tasks that they had. For example, as far as command was concerned, and operative tasks, the assistant commander for operations would talk about that, or the Chief of Staff would, because that is their line of work; then, after that, somebody from the operations and training department would discuss the plan; then the assistant Chief of Staff for mobilisation and replenishment would talk about manning losses and all other problems that had to be resolved; then the assistant commander for morale; then the assistant commander for logistics would report. And with regard to security questions and tasks related to security, it was the chief of security who reported, or rather, the assistant commander for security. At the end, the Chief of Staff would propose the tasks for the following day and then the commander would adopt that and he would say what the focus would be, what the focal tasks would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you go to these meetings regularly?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every time I was called, I went.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think we can continue now. If Mr. Moore has any further questions about these matters, I'm sure he's going to avail himself of the right to ask the questions in his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to pick up where we left off yesterday. I'd like to have MFI 3D050027 brought up in e-court. This is a document produced by the security administration dated the 15th of October, 1991. The 65 ter number is 3D04.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Briefly about this document, Mr. Sljivancanin, speaking of what you were talking about a while ago, 65 ter 3D04 and 3D050027, that is the e-court reference. Who is this document addressed to, Mr. Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see anything on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. I thought you had it in front of you.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we can blow it up a little. Who was this document sent to, if you look at the heading?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was sent by the assistant chief of security of the chef du cabinet of the federal ministry. It was sent to the command of the Guards Brigade and the addressee is the chief of the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think the document speaks for itself. It is obvious that something is being submitted to the security administration, and what I really want to know about is, further down, it says "Operations Groups for Work with Prisoners" and their composition. Tell me, please, what did your security organs do with any prisoners, exactly? And as far as there were prisoners, what exactly was the procedure?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can explain this document briefly. I'm looking at this now and I see that this is a document produced by the security administration. The security administration is the focal point for tactics, for equipping the military police units with military equipment, and they work closely together with other focal points in the military police in terms of weapons and equipment. This document was sent for me to write exactly where the military police units were deployed, what their strength was, what their assignments were exactly, so that the administration, as the focal point, could send enough weapons, could adjust the manpower levels, and that sort of thing. As for any POWs, or rather, perpetrators of crimes, which is what we called them at the time, we were ordered by the commander and by the administration, in the specialist technical terms, and the issue of those people was an issue for the commands and not just for the security organ and the military police. We were told that, should we find any such people, they were to be taken to Sid directly, to some sort of collection centre, where they were worked with from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll see about that later. Which of your associates were members of these operative groups, or was there anyone?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the assignment was underway to lift the siege of the barracks, the only place where civilians were being collected was some sort of triage and vetting, if you like, where screening was performed. There was the Velepromet facility where my own subordinate security organs sometimes took part in these technical and specialist tasks, more specifically Captain Srecko Borisavljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 821, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document that I would like to see is document with the e-court reference 3D050165; the 65 ter reference is 3D37. This is entitled "Information," dated the 22nd of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will not be dwelling on this document for long but there is one thing I want to know. Tell us what it's about. Who produced this document, and on based on whose information?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We looked at a document just like this one yesterday. That was also produced by the chief of security of the cabinet of the Federal Secretary based on information that I had sent them from our area of operations, and I forwarded it to the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now that we're going through it, can you please comment on the first two paragraphs on the screen. What was the subject of your security analysis and security processing throughout the Vukovar operation?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: While combat operations were still underway in Vukovar and the siege was being lifted of the barracks, there were all sorts of issues being raised about our work, but there were also all these other issues affecting morale and impairing the combat-readiness of the units; that means any sort of enemy activity aimed against these units. In other words, there was no issue that did not concern me, as the chief of the security organ. Here we see comments about irregular work being performed by artillery units, and if you want me to, I can explain that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that later once we start analysing.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the second paragraph, there is talk of a peace, anonymity and defeatism in a unit of the 2nd Battalion, where soldiers started expressing their discontent on a massive scale with how combat operations were going, and also the question of dismissing some of the reservists because they had already been with the unit for over 45 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is something you mentioned yesterday, but just to specify for the benefit of the Chamber: What exactly was your position regarding this decision of the government of the Republic of Serbia to dismiss the reservists and send them away from the front line? How did that affect the security-related issues that you were in charge of?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then, as now, I believe that the Guards Motorised Brigade was a unit of the armed forces of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. I believe that decisions taken by the defence minister of the Republic of Serbia did not apply to us under the constitution as it was at the time. I thought that applied to the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Serbia rather than to us. So I demanded from the commander that this decision not be complied with and that all the mobilised fighters who arrived there as part of our overall units stay there until the completion of the task, and that the young soldiers, the junior soldiers be withdrawn. I met with a great deal of resistance about this with the reservists, the Motorised Battalion, and also some volunteers who started pointing their weapons at me, that sort of thing. Eventually, I also met with the reluctance of the assistant commander for moral guidance. I had to go and talk to him, I had to go and see him, and he explained to me that we simply had to comply with this one. And that's where my influence stopped. There was nothing more I could do. It had to be complied with, but those were my proposals at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Page 2 of this document, if we can look at paragraph 1, talks about a man named Miroslav Macura. Again, there is reference here to your own operative work or intelligence work.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is one of the ways that intelligence was gathered about arms smuggling and selling weapons. We took steps for all such persons involved in such activities to be identified and for legal steps to be taken against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have a number for this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 822.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document is the document that I wish to discuss, but please, can we go into private session because there is mention of a protected witness in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps the document could be brought up on the screen for the benefit of the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What can you see in the second and third paragraphs, Mr. Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second paragraph talks about volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Quite right. What exactly went on there, and what did you do about it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a lot being said about these volunteers. It's a long story. I could go on until the cows come home. As members of the Guards Brigade, we wanted to restore order and discipline, to the extent that it was possible under the conditions, and to the extent that it was possible with -- those people had been sent over to work with us. It wasn't us who came up with the idea of volunteers. We received the assistance of volunteers just in order to have the manpower levels brought up in the reserve forces. Whoever came up with that, please come forward and say so. This is not something that I can speak about. It was somebody from the Superior Command. We were just fighting there. So the idea was for order and discipline to be restored to the ranks of those fighters. And those we couldn't manage, we tried to get them to be reasonable, to some extent. We sent reports about this, and there is a report here saying that we sent back 70 volunteers. This report says we, at one point, sent back 70 volunteers, and that on the 24th we would be returning another 20 who had previously joined the Guards Motorised Brigade because of their mental instability, because of their erroneous understanding of the task at hand, and because of their lack of discipline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Your answers are long and they are delivered very quickly. To give the interpreters more chance, if you could keep them shorter and slower. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The next paragraph refers to a search that was conducted and that certain things were found. I'm not going to ask you about that. I guess this was a regular procedure when such persons went away from the zone of combat operations; right? And please be brief.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a very precise and clear-cut procedure. No one could take out any weapons or any equipment from that zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a number for this document, which I propose to tender under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 823, under seal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now we are going to go to a document of the 25th of October, 1991. Actually, these are two documents, but let us go to the first one. First, that is a letter by the assistant chief of security as a covering document and then a letter by the administration of -- security administration of the 25th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have the e-court reference right now. I believe that everyone has it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter is 3D09, but if the Chamber does not have it before them, then I could -- so it's 3D050205 in e-court. Can we zoom in on this, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is this in terms of form; will you tell us? And then we shall go to the next document of which this is a covering document.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see under seal that this is the assistant of the chief of cabinet for security -- of the cabinet of the Federal Secretary for National Defence submitting a memorandum informing about certain information of events in Vukovar, and it refers to the small number of loyal Croats, "loyal" in inverted commas.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we now see the next document. Do you have it before you, Mr. Sljivancanin, the report of the security administration, or do we have to bring it up on the screen? Of the 25th of October, 1991, that is.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to find it here but I'm unable to.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could it please also be put on the e-court for our benefit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Of course, inadvertent errors are possible with this volume of documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you? Okay. All right. Thank you. When you look at the previous document, it actually refers to this document quite clearly. I should like you to comment on the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of security of the cabinet of the Federal Secretary received a letter from the administration for security and he assisted -- it was an important document for the work of the security organ in the Guards Brigade as it referred to the zone where we were. And he referred that document to the security administration, and its second paragraph says: "One of the centres of defence of the National Guards Corps and the MUP is the Vukovar Hospital, on the premises of which are housed members of the National Guards Corps, whereas MUP members have been accommodated at a police station. The most extreme of butchers have been accommodated in the rooms of the former neuropsychiatry ward, and a number of the medical staff of the Vukovar Hospital are also involved in the commission of crimes."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you get such a memorandum, according to this technical line, is this a sort of guideline for work for you? And what kind of a guideline is it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Evidence has already been presented here regarding the log entries of the war log of the Guards Brigade, where the reconnaissance organs of our 1st Battalion had a similar report already in October. At that time, the Vukovar Hospital was not in the zone of operations of the Guards Brigade, but I informed, of this document, our commander and the core command at a meeting, and I also informed of it the subordinate commanders so that they would also work on collecting information. And I gave instructions for operational work to my subordinated security organs for further data gathering.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe, Your Honours, that these two documents could be tendered as a single exhibit; and if not, then perhaps as two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As we don't have copies of them, I think it will be better if they were separate. We are told that your wish is met because in e-court they've been made into one document, so they will have one number collectively.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And the number will be 824, Your Honour, so Exhibit 824.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see report of the organ of security of the 25th of October. This is 3D05211, 3D10. And we will have to go into private session again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, according to the line of security, did you generally receive information about the situation in the war theatre about units of the adversary and relevant information for combat operation in terms of security? And from whom did you get some information?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the information which I received had to do with counter-intelligence measures and security from the chief of security of the cabinet of the Federal Secretary and from nobody else, as I've already said. We have seen the memo that he sent me about the situation in the Vukovar Hospital, and there were other such reports and memorandums which we used for further operational work and for direction of the units in the zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have given me this answer but I will repeat: Did you get such information from the organs of security of the 1st Military District?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have repeatedly said, from no one else, from no one else did I get any information, including from the security organ of the 1st Military District. I only received professional advice from General Vasiljevic when he stayed in the zone of combat operations. So I received information from no one else from the chief of security of the cabinet of the Federal Secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During your stay at the Vukovar front, did you have any direct contacts or via communication centres with Mr. Mile Babic and Mr. Ljubisa Petkovic? And the Chamber knows that these are the chief and assistant chief for security of the 1st Military District.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no contacts whatsoever with these two men, either during the combat operations, before them, or ever after those.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you, during your stay in Vukovar, hear, as you have heard people testify before this Court, about events in Ilok, Sarengrad, Lovas and other places of Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I heard about this was from the documents which were presented to this august Tribunal, and before that, I had had no information about that at all. And, frankly speaking, I was preoccupied with the discharge of my duty assigned to us as a unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at another document which is a document which, in e-court, is marked in the system 3D050054; in the 65 ter list, it is document 3D12. That is a letter of the security administration of the 5th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I should just like to read this first part and then the end and ask you for your comment. So this is a letter of the security administration, sent through the cabinet of the assistant for security of the SSNO to the security organ of the Guards Brigade. It says: "On the 3rd of November, 1991, the commander of the Vukovar Defence Staff, M. Dedakovic, aka Jastreb, stated in a conversation with F. Tudjman that the ZNG and MUP forces in this town were in a very difficult situation; that a JNA unit (8 tanks and infantry) had penetrated to the port silos and hospital sector, i.e., near the shelters of the ZNG and MUP that he has not received ammunition." It goes on to speak about this intercepted conversation on the next page, page 2. It refers to the purpose of the submission of this document. Tell me, do you remember this? And what was done in connection with it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember the document. This is also a document which, like the previous one, arrived. I informed the command [Realtime transcript read in error "combat"] the core [Realtime transcript read in error "corps"] command, headed by the commander of the Guards Brigade; I informed my own security officers. What is important to say in this regard is that data of -- to the security organ does not come from just one chief, it comes from a number of sides to the organs of security, to the administration of security, which then undertakes an analysis to see whether they are true or not. It has to have a number of sources because some information can be planted or misinformation or simply incorrect. So information which is established to be correct is sent to the structures, to the units in that zone, in order for them to plan their further combat missions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I don't know if it's a question of translation. I'm looking at 23, 7, and the way I have it doesn't agree with what we understand. It is: "I informed the combat -- the core command, headed by the commander of the Guards Brigade ..." I wonder if my learned friend -- it doesn't make sense, I would have thought, just on a common sense basis, whether that could be clarified, if my learned friend would mind doing that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me, if the interpreter can explain. It's "core command," c-o-r-e command, the core command staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank Mr. Moore. It was obviously a translation mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, this is because you speak too fast.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I, as the assistant commander for security of the Guards Motorised Brigade, with documents of this kind and similar documents, had a meeting with a commander; would always inform the commander and the core, c-o-r-e, command staff whose -- namely, his assistants in the command of the Guards Motorised Brigade, in order for that information to be used for further use of the units and the planning of combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A moment ago you mentioned in private session the arrival of Mr. Vasiljevic. Now, in public session, just be careful about that particular part. What was it that he wanted? And were you present when he was there? I think this was the second time that he came.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the way it was: I remembered it well. General Aca Vasiljevic came to Vukovar, or rather, to the zone that was then under the control of the Guards Motorised Brigade three times. The first time he came in the month of October; the second time also in late October or perhaps the beginning ever November - I cannot remember the exact date; and the third time he came - perhaps I remember that date better - during the visit of -- or rather, the day when Mr. Vance was in Vukovar, but he came in the evening. General Vasiljevic was highly disciplined, a fair officer, and what his tasks were, that is to say, why he came, I don't know exactly. Every time he came, he first contacted the commander, and I always found him with the commander. They would invite me to come into the commander's premises. After the talks he had with the commander - and I really don't know what they talked about - he would come to the rooms where I was and he would give me advice in terms of professional guidance with regard to counter-intelligence. He also criticised me in terms of some of the work I was doing where I was exposed perhaps more than I should have. I have already referred to the example of General Adzic's visit. He also asked me for my observations regarding security in the Guards Motorised Brigade. Those were primarily the matters that he discussed then. During his second stay, when I told him about the security situation in the 1st Battalion of the military police, and the problem of Witness P01, since Mr. Aca Vasiljevic knew him as well, when some intelligence work was being done by them, when they had some intelligence assignments that they were on, he wanted to go and talk to him. I advised him not to go, that we would solve the question, but he did go and I know that then, those questions related to their dissatisfaction were not involved. I've already explained how they were resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why did you advise him not to go to the unit?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I advised him not to go then because of the rumours and stories that were being bandied about even among the members of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army and because I thought that at that moment these people were tired, and that once they got some rest we would find solutions that would make it possible to resolve matters in an easier manner. There were occurrences at that time that many high-ranking officers of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army - how should I put this? - well, they deserted or left the units of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army. And this was being talked about all the time - who was a traitor, who no longer believed in the JNA, and so on. And now I can tell the honourable Trial Chamber and all of you this: When General Vasiljevic attended this meeting, in that unit, there was an exceptionally honourable and honest man in that unit, a Croat, Ivo Pavkovic, an officer, who taught me as well what kind of officer I should be. He had two sons who were NCOs, and he brought both of them out on this mission. Officers were putting questions regarding some statement made by Admiral Grubesic, the commander of the navy, as to why he had deserted. The general tried to explain to them, justifying this by saying that it was his children who lived in Split that talked him into it. Mr. Ivo Pavkovic said the following, and I remember his words: "Comrade General, I am a Croat, and I was born in a village near Sibenik." I cannot remember the exact name of the village now. "And I have an argument with all my local villagers and my family because I think that Yugoslavia is a country where we can all live happily together, and now you are justifying what the general did by saying that he listened to his children." So I'm trying to say that this is what was being discussed at the front line and what people were saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move on to an exhibit now, 749.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Is my learned friend going to make 3D12 an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could this document, dated the 5th of November, 1991, be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 825, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 749. Could we please display the second page. I would be interested in this third, fourth paragraph. Could we have it up a bit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is an official report from Operations Group South. It's going up to their superiors and there is a reference to what you talked about a few moments ago and that is the problem related to combat morale. Mr. Sljivancanin, just tell me one thing: From the aspect of security organs, how important is discipline and morale and not to have defeatism and desertion? How important is that from the point of view of security?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is important with regard to all questions, not only security; in terms of command in general. Defeatism, morale, desertion, if that kind of thing happens in units, or rather, if there is a drop in morale, then the command cannot have any kind of task carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know, since, in your unit, there was an assistant commander for morale and information - his name was already mentioned - was he, like you, often at the front line? And did he have first-hand information about these things that we have been discussing?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just add one more thing in respect to this document? In my reports, there is a reference to this problem of morale in the 20th Partisan Brigade and the armoured battalion of the 544th, and now you see that it's being referred to in this report as well. As for the assistant commander for morale, throughout the operation regarding the deblockade of the barracks, I never saw him anywhere except for the village of Negoslavci. Now, whether he went anywhere else, I don't know; but I never came across him anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please look at a document which is marked in e-court 3D050701, and the 65 ter number is 3D38. There is an accompanying letter as well. Information about members of the MUP and the ZNG in Vukovar. Again, as far as I can see, this is another document submitted to the security administration. Could we have page 10 of the B/C/S on the screen, and in English, it is page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, generally speaking, what this document is, Mr. Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a similar document but it's much lengthier. It was compiled by the security administration on the basis of information accessible to it from different sources regarding the network of rebel paramilitary forces in Vukovar and their formations, names, as well as groupings at different points where they were that were supposed to be used by the further intelligence work of the organs that were in that zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What it says here is something that I'm going to read. "Certain information indicates that the nuclear and similar shelters being used by the Croatian paramilitary formations are located as follows: Number 1, shelter located in the middle of Olajnica; then the cellar in Vukovar PU; and number 3, the cellar between the old and new hospitals, which, according to some intelligence, contains about 200 wounded. According to some estimates, there could be another 50 people sheltering there. The hospital is guarded by about 7 ZNG members." Was this important information for your own intelligence work?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's perhaps late in the day, but I would object to this particular document unless the groundwork has been laid, because as far as I can understand it, this is not a document that was either created as a result of Mr. Sljivancanin's work or that he was a recipient of the document, and consequently, his knowledge of the document has to be established before he, surely, can comment on it vis-a-vis the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, maybe I was moving too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, tell us what it is that you know about this document. What Mr. Moore asked, did you create this document or did somebody else create this document and did you just come across it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, like the other documents came in, the ones that we read here about the commanders, talks with Tudjman, and information about what is in the hospital, and so on and so forth, this document comes from the security administration, as they compiled information from different sides. And they know where they collected this information through security organs. And it was sent to the chief of security of the cabinet to the Federal Secretary and then he forwarded that document to me. The procedure was the same like with other documents. First, it is used in intelligence work of the security organs that are subordinated to me, and I informed the commander and command of the Guards Motorised Brigade about excerpts from this document that are used for planning combat actions. These paragraphs that you read out just now say that intelligence information collected then, even before the blockade of the barracks, and the final disarmament of paramilitary formations were correct and according to witness -- witnesses who appeared before this Court said the same thing. They talked about the shelter in Olajnica, they talked about the agricultural farm and where people were being put up, and they talked about the cellars between the two hospitals in Vukovar; that is to say, that the security administration, by its own methods and through its own work, collected this information that was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that this has been clarified, and I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 826, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to stop with documents now and we are going to talk about a completely different subject, but we will go back to this. I would like for you to testify now, or actually we're going to take a break but then we're going to move on to a subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, regarding the evacuation of wounded from the Vukovar Hospital, your name was being referred to, so I would like to ask you: What was it that was going on there? We heard about two convoys in evidence here. What happened the first time? What happened the second time? Would you start first ...

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once the siege had been lifted and the paramilitaries had been disarmed, on about the 10th of October, an order came from the Superior Command. I would like for you at the end to ask me about my conversation with Marin Vidic about this matter. An order came from the Superior Command to cease all operations and, over the following two or three days, to receive a humanitarian convoy on its way to Vukovar. They said that convoy should be used to evacuate all the wounded from the town. The command of the Guards Brigade, headed by the commander and all the senior officers, did whatever it could to stop the fighting at the cost of sustaining the greatest losses up until that point. And, indeed, we complied with the cease-fire. On the 13th of November, rather, the 13th of October -- my mistake, I apologise. Somebody might be wondering how come I remember the date. Because I have a document that I believe you will be showing later on. The commander, Mr. Mrksic, determined the tasks and handed the tasks out to Colonel Pavkovic and myself, telling us to go to the village of Marinci to take over the convoy from units of the 1st Guards Division and to bring it back to Vukovar in the safest possible way as well as to allow it to cross into the area under the control of Croat paramilitaries. I used the radio that I told you about yesterday; I explained yesterday how I had got hold of it. And I repeatedly called the commander of the Croat paramilitary forces on that day, pleading with him to create conditions that were safe for those people who were coming in to help them. However, more often than not, they would not react. This fell on deaf ears. They carried out acts of provocation and they fired at us. It wasn't before that afternoon that we got the convoy safe, as far as the Vukovar Hospital. Again, we called the commander of the Croat paramilitary forces to open up a passage for the convoy to take the asphalt road down the Sajmiste Street all the way up to the downtown area. There's one thing that I wish to say now about something that I saw on the Zagreb TV last year, something they like to refer to as the commemoration of the fall of Vukovar. The programme is called Latinica, and there was this commander who was called to that programme and he stated this verbatim, "The convoy was not allowed to pass because Sljivancanin wanted to use his cunning in order to enter Vukovar in tanks," which is the worst piece of nonsense I've heard of in ages. That's not what I was thinking about at the time, nor did I have any tanks under my command. Still, they did not allow the convoy through and the convoy had to spend that night at the Vukovar barracks. There were about 100 vehicles in that convoy - trucks, medical vehicles, carrying supplies and all the other necessities. This convoy was led by a person named Robert Michel. We members of the Guards Brigade did our best to make sure conditions were safe for them and to allow the convoy to enter Vukovar. During that night, fire was opened on the barracks, so the people driving those vehicles and accompanying the convoy got scared. They asked for the convoy to be sent back. I remained adamant that they should drive into Vukovar and the commander was adamant, too. We called the command of the 1st Military District, specifically General Panic. He decided that since they had refused to proceed, they should be sent back, and we were to make sure they got back to Vinkovci safe. This task was far harder than the task of bringing the convoy in. I talked to Robert Michel and I said we'd do everything, but I said what I wanted in return from him was a certificate saying that we had done all within our power. And he said he would oblige as soon as we got the convoy as far as Vinkovci, the perimeter of the Vinkovci area. When we reached the villages of Marinci, we faced a great deal of trouble with the locals and the village's TO. They virtually were hellbent on attacking the convoy and all the people there. Their main reason, at least that's the way they painted the situation, was the day before we escorted the convoy through the village, Croat paramilitary forces had entered the village and committed a massacre. So what they were saying now was, "We are burying our own people today that were killed yesterday because of the convoy, and you JNA traitors are doing nothing but helping the Croats along." That was a difficult situation. So, again, I'm coming back to the Latinica programme on Croatian TV, the one that I saw last year, where Mr. Paraga and the commander of the Croatian forces both stated that on the 13th, at 6.00, they had initiated a breakaway through the village of Marinci and then on to Vukovar. They tried to break through and they showed a document to that effect, allegedly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the break can we just look at another document.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please allow me to finish. We managed to safely get the convoy back. The convoy drove back into Croatia without having accomplished its mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just another document, 3D010060, one last document before the break. We have it in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, you know what we are about to bring up on the screen, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Is this a 3D Defence document working on the Defence number or is it an exhibit? Because I've just got the one number. Normally we get 3D37 or 36 or 25. Does my learned friend have that particular number? It would help enormously.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is ID 3D010060. There, it's on our screens right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, that's the English. I'm not asking you to read it. We know there's a B/C/S version, too. What is this, in a nutshell, please?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a certificate that I was issued personally by Mr. Michel, in his own hand, on the 14th of October, 1991, in the village of Marinci, when the convoy was returned to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the document was then translated into B/C/S. Can we please have the B/C/S admitted into evidence; the English, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Both will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: With exhibit reference 827, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's time for our break, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, could you please keep your answers as brief as possible. As Judge Parker has noticed, we have a lot of different subjects to go through and we have a lot of important things to say, so please bear that in mind. If necessary, we can raise further issues in redirect. For the time being, let's stick to what is really important. Now let us move on to that second evacuation in October, if we can call it that. What happened several days later, if you can give us a brief description?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several days later, after that first convoy failed to go through, again, Colonel Pavkovic and I received an assignment from the commander to meet a new convoy in the village of Marinci. Again, the convoy was led by Robert Michel and it comprised a lot less vehicles than the first time around. There were about 30, mostly medical vehicles and the odd small truck; no trailers this time around. Again, he asked that the convoy take the road through the village of Bogdanovci. Like the first time around, we warned him that the road was booby-trapped and that the village was under the control of the Croat paramilitary units. We said we could take him near that village but no further than that. We showed him the map to indicate where we would be waiting for him so that they might be escorted from Bogdanovci to Vukovar. This is the area around elevation 102, along the road, the village of Bogdanovci, in the Vukovar area. He agreed, saying that he had another commitment to take someone along who was waiting in the village of Bogdanovci; I don't know who that was. We took them near the village. They took a different road from there. We went back and informed Commander Mrksic about this. I don't remember exactly what Mrksic told us but I know that he, too, later went with us to elevation 102 to see if the convoy would reach Vukovar safely. We had received orders from our own Superior Command that no fire must be opened and that we had to make sure the convoy got into Vukovar. We complied with that decision. When we reached elevation 102, as far as I remember, there was a unit deployed there. It was a unit of the armoured battalion of the 212th Mechanised Brigade. I might be off the mark, but I think that was the unit that was there. I know the commander informed the battalion commander that the convoy had not got through. We were concerned about this because we were responsible for this convoy. I don't know what tasks the commander then issued to the commander of the armoured battalion, but he should have exercised better control over his own territory at the time. That is certain. We waited there, and after some time the convoy emerged from the direction of Vukovar. They were travelling through some cornfields. I could indicate that on the map that we used. It was preceded by a car bearing a -- white Zastava car, a white Zastava 101. The people walking ahead of the convoy opened fire on the soldiers manning a tank. They left the Zastava car behind, ran out, and started running through the cornfield. Commander Mrksic then ordered that no one was to open fire, regardless of the fact that we had been fired at, that those people had fired at our soldiers. We never found out who the persons from that vehicle were. The convoy stopped right there. A group of officers descended from elevation 102 and went into the cornfield where we met up with Robert Michel. We got the convoy as far as elevation 102, the asphalt road leading from Bogdanovci to Vukovar, and Commander Mrksic had a word with Mr. Robert Michel. He explained, as far as I remember, that he had been derailed, as it were, by the people in Bogdanovci to a village road, and that was the reason he had not been able to comply with what had been agreed. But they had difficulty with this minefield, he said. Nonetheless, he asked us to show him the best asphalt road that they could now take to go back to Bogdanovci, because apparently he had some people there in Bogdanovci that he had left behind, people from the convoy, and that he now needed to pick up. The commander showed him the road - I can indicate that on the map - and the conversation was over. They headed out. They took that road back to Bogdanovci. Colonel Pavkovic and I were supposed to take the long way around, through the village of Petrovci, and arrive outside the village of Bogdanovci to take them further to the village of Marinci from where they would eventually be able to return to Croatia. About 800 metres away from where we were, in the direction of the village of Bogdanovci, we heard an explosion, and I remember clearly the fifth vehicle in that column was blown up. So the first four got through, but the fifth vehicle was a vehicle belonging to the international observers, the international monitors. So what we feared most eventually happened. We feared that someone might provoke an accident or something like that so that they might be able to say that the JNA units were hampering the international monitors, yet again. This time around, two ladies, or a lady, was wounded. I'm not quite certain. I do know for a fact, though, that immediately a JNA ambulance came and took them to the Negoslavci hospital. From there, they were taken by helicopter to the Military Medical Academy in Belgrade. Robert Michel returned and asked for the JNA to again take charge of that convoy. The commander offered for him to take the asphalt road to Vukovar and then down another asphalt road to the village of Petrovci and on to Sid. Robert Michel said he was willing to go to the village of Petrovci but was not willing to go back to Vukovar; rather, while being shown the map, and we indicated to him the distance between these two places, he chose a plain or some sort of a village road and he wanted to take that road and the asphalt road to the village of Petrovci. Commander Mrksic agreed. Our members of command returned and I was ordered to stay behind with some military policemen who would make sure they were safe until they reached the asphalt road and were on their way back to the area under the control of the 1st Guards Division, near the village of Petrovci. Once they were on their way - it was raining heavily; this was afternoon of that day - the vehicles got bogged down on that dirt track and they couldn't move forward or, indeed, turn back. We tried to free those vehicles by using APCs and we spent the whole night doing that until we got them back to the Petrovci road. I exchanged greetings with Mr. Michel. We were all soaked to our skin. Then, at one point, one of these vehicles disgorged one of our soldiers whom I had been looking for, someone who had gone missing on the 2nd of October. He had recognised the voices of his own fellow soldiers who were pulling those vehicles out by using APCs. The name of this soldier is Zivkovic, and he was a member of the armoured battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's pause there for a while. You keep mentioning to the village of -- we keep mentioning the village of Bogdanovci. Under whose firepower, as it were, was the village of Bogdanovci? Who was controlling that village at the time?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village of Bogdanovci, all the way up until the 18th or possibly the 15th of November, remained under the control of the Croat paramilitary forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Based on your information, what exactly brought about this explosion and caused those ladies in the convoy to be hurt or injured? Who provoked that incident?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was one of the defenders of that village. We later realised, when we arrived, they placed a mine from the cornfield underneath that vehicle and the grenade was placed under the fifth vehicle in that convoy, consisting of international monitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please place on our screens the map marked ZA004292.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I cannot find this document in e-court. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, please. 3D0060009. This is one of the documents which we received in the OTP's disclosure and it accompanied the reports of the European Monitoring Mission at the time, so that I do not know who is the author or what has been drawn in the map, but I think that it is useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, let us not repeat the entire story. Just draw in the sector which was controlled by the paramilitary units of Croatia. Where did you wait for them? Where is this elevation point? And where did this incident, i.e., suffering, occur?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The elevation point 102 is right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we zoom in on this map, please.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I said elevation 102.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we could go on now and then ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I show it on the map in Exhibit 156?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether Mr. Sljivancanin has a paper map in front of him which we could place on the ELMO and then try to proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, then, perhaps that would be the best way to proceed. Put it on the ELMO and then use that copy and then tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said elevation point 102 is right here. Should I mark it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mark it with number 1.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I shall draw a line here to indicate it, so 1. The village of Bogdanovci, which was controlled by the paramilitary forces of Croatia, was right here, in this part. More or less, this is it. Lusac, this was under their control. Outside this line was under the control of the Croatian paramilitary forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Put number 2 there, and thereby you are showing whether it is true whether, from there, they had access to Vukovar, a link with Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had a link via this field road by the Vuka River through Lusac and on. Evidence has been presented here time and again and a lot has been said about it. So the village of Marinci, shall I mark that, too?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village of Marinci is here, marked with a number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And that was under whose control?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the zone of operations of the 1st Guards Motorised Division. They held that village, and when we met that convoy at this cross roads, they took the turn to Bogdanovci. They went to Bogdanovci, and, as Robert Michel told us later, they took this road along the River Vuka, towards Vukovar, from Bogdanovci. He did not take the asphalt road where we were waiting for him at elevation 102. And the convoy returned from Vukovar. He took this road here, this direction, towards elevation 102, and that is this area number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the talk with the commander, he set off in this direction, and that is indicated by arrow number 5, towards the village of Bogdanovci. After the mine incident, they returned to the elevation point 102, and at night, I took them in this direction, marked by 6, to the asphalt road, pulling them out of the asphalt road towards the village of Petrovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mark by a number 7 where the explosion occurred.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I shall put a point there and then I shall draw an arrow. This is more or less where this explosion happened. Perhaps it was closer to the village. So it is marked by number 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we tender this into evidence, extract it from this batch, and Mr. Sljivancanin will not be needing this particular paper anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 828, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at a short video clip, some video footage, in connection with this. That is a video clip which is part of the V document -- of the video document, V000-5034.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] On this road here, you could have passed by the asphalt road with all of our best regards, because we do not want the wounded in Vukovar to die but to be pulled out. We waited for you and you are taking secret roads, danger roads, to endanger your own lives and the lives of the wounded. [In English] Withdraw from this town as much as possible wounded people."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is this, and who was talking here? Who is this dialogue between?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a dialogue of Commander Mrksic and Mr. Robert Michel, and I believe that this was a conversation which took place at elevation point 102. I don't know the exact date right now, but some four days must have elapsed since the day of the first convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we tender this video into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 829, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Speaking of the date, let us take a look at one exhibit which is related to this and wrap up this topic. It is Exhibit 327, which I should like to ask to be placed on the screen. Page 2 of the B/C/S version, that is a report of the command of the 1st Army District, 1st Military District, of the 19th of October, 1991, number 832-85/115. If we can bring up page 2, the bottom part. This is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us read the text. Is this a report which pertains to and does it describe what you have just testified about? You can read it to yourself or you can read it out, if you prefer.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can read it out, if need be, but this is a report which pertains exactly to what I have been describing, and this document shows that it took place on the 19th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a report of the 19th of October, and a lot about it has been said in the war log of the Guards Brigade with a precise timetable of the events that happened. And perhaps we will be taking a look at that, too, but now we shall move on to another topic. You obviously had frequent contacts with journalists during your stay in Vukovar. Can I ask you why, and how come? And how was it organised?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, during the execution of combat operations and the lifting of the blockade on the barracks in Vukovar, it is true that I had frequent encounters with the press. First of all, journalists were always curious to come and -- come by the most recent information in connection with the execution of combat operations. There have been different testimonies about me here and I am not hiding this fact. From the first day, I was, throughout the day, on the front line and I toured all the troops of the Motorised Guards Brigade, in particular the young soldiers from the 2nd Battalion of the military police and the 2nd Motorised Battalion, because these were soldiers who were just completing their third month of their combat training and had not completed their full combat training by that time. Combat training was supposed to last five months and 22 days, according to our teaching curricula and plans at that time, but they were not fortunate enough, seeing -- in view of everything that had befallen us, and they had to go and carry out this mission that was assigned to us. I regarded all those soldiers - and I was relatively young at that time - as my own sons, and it was really hard for me -- it would have been hard for me if anything had happened to any of them. So by my presence, I wanted sometimes to draw their attention to the fact that -- because they were playing like children, you know, that they should be wary, lest some surprises happened. Secondly, I was at the front line, as I have said at the beginning, and I really did my level best to learn any and all information about our soldiers who went missing in order to liberate them and return them to the unit. And I was also at the front line because I very often was called by senior commanding officers whom I knew from Belgrade or from other garrisons in the territory of Yugoslavia, and sometimes also people called me from the command of the 1st Military District, very often, I have to say, including senior commanding officers who were Croats, who asked me to find some of their kin, relatives, and members of their families and to send them to Sid, if I could. And I did that. So the journalists, when they came to the front line -- and there was, by the way, a press centre in Negoslavci. The press centre was managed by Captain Radojica Zvorcan, who, for a while, was the commander of a military police company in the 1st Battalion of the military police when I was the commander of that battalion, and he asked me to help me out, saying that the assistant for morale would not come to the front line. And he asked for assistance to help him actually direct the journalists and respond to their requests. As all of these were accredited journalists who had been issued permits from the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, I considered that we had nothing to hide from them and that we, as members of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army, were doing everything publicly, irrespective of the fact that I was the chief of security, that we wanted to help every person and every citizen of our country.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have any contacts and did you have this position when it came to the treatment of foreign journalists as well at that time?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, I was even more cooperative when it came to foreign journalists and I took more pains to provide their security than when it came to journalists who came from our country. And I always did my best to be available, to be there for them, to show them everything that we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see the document marked 3D010058 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until it comes up on the screen, I can also add this: I remember on one occasion, personally, the chief of the cabinet of the Federal Secretary, Mr. Vuk Obranovic, asked, through the commander, through Mr. Mrksic, that a team of journalists, led by Mr. van Lynden, a journalist who took the stand here, for them to spend the night at the positions of our units and to be with us. And, with permission from my commander, I personally took him to the anti-terrorist unit and I spent the entire night with them in order to prevent anything from happening to them. And they spent the night on those positions with those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, this document is in English but I believe that you are familiar with it. What is this, and what did you get it? If you did get it, how did you come by it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Upon returning from Vukovar, and during the execution of missions in Vukovar, I received letters from different people, including journalists, and I remember very well this document. I received this letter whilst still in Vukovar. I remember that it was the 4th of November, the day of the Guards Motorised Brigade. The letter was sent to me by a British journalist who was staying in Vukovar and had contact with me during his stay in Vukovar. And this is the letter and I'm still keeping it and I'm glad that I still have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 830, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go into private session for a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We saw from the video footage and we heard from testimony that you had direct contact with international organisations as well and with the International Red Cross. Very soon we are going to move on to those dates that we are particularly interested in. But I would like to ask you the following: Before the 18th of November, did you have any contact with Mr. Borsinger, first and foremost, and what kind of contacts were they, during the war operations, during combat?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for Mr. Nicholas Borsinger, I had contacts with him from sometime in mid-October until the ultimate -- or rather, until the 21st of November, in the evening, every day in Vukovar. Mr. Borsinger -- actually, a day would not go by without him coming to see me for an hour or two and without me taking him along the front line in Vukovar. And he spent most of his time in Velepromet, in the centre, where civilians came at the time. And he said that he would help in terms of bringing food supplies, medicine, and so on. Unfortunately, he didn't bring anything ever, except for that one time we went to the Vukovar Hospital. I was on very friendly, very good terms with him. Later on, we remained on friendly terms as well. I never feel that our relationship was impaired in any way. If Mr. Borsinger is listening to this somewhere now, I'm asking him to come forth and to say the truth, whether this is the truth. I tried to help him do everything that he intended. I even did not ask the commander for permission, and sometimes I even went apart from regulations. I found a house near the press centre and I asked Captain Radojica Zvorcan to always make it possible for him and his team to spend the night at the house, if necessary. And, indeed, for these international organisations, if I had a good relationship with anyone, it was with Mr. Nicholas Borsinger.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, I would just like to deal with the war diary as quickly as possible and then let us move on to the events that everyone here is interested in the most. Just a few entries in the war diary and I believe that you are a relevant witness for this. So please let us move on to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is Exhibit 401. The B/C/S version is 02935465. Actually, I'd like to ask for something else, if we can deal with this in a chronological manner. The B/C/S page is 13-02935446, the entry from the 4th of October at 12.00. Page 13. The B/C/S. Right. Thank you. The English, page 12. The 4th of the October, at 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, can you see that entry?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. I understand the difficulties. We don't have such an entry on our copy. Is it possible to put it on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have that entry either.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. I have it right in front of me. The pages are a bit mixed up here. I'll tell you, the English version -- well, all right, it's the right entry here on the screen, and in English here it is, 0100507. We've already made comments about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have it now, fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We've already made comments with regard to this entry.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here it says the village of Negoslavci, 1200 hours, the 4th of October.
