"The reconnaissance organs of the 1st Motorised Battalion have reported that in the old and the new hospitals is the Ustasha headquarters that is underground." I already made comments on that with regard to the reports from the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, in your view, how far away were Jastreb's headquarters? We're going to talk about that later. How far away from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was personally in that shelter on the 19th, in the evening, and on the 20th, in the afternoon and in the morning. This is the 19th and 20th of November. And I can measure it in steps, say it is 200 or 300 metres at the most. That's the distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move on to another entry. That is 02935457. The English version -- the B/C/S version is page 24, rather, and the English version is page 22. The entry is dated the 11th of October; the time is 1645 hours. I'm going to read it out. The handwriting is quite illegible, so I imagine that the English version will be more readily understandable.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "Received order of the command of the 1st IKM Military District, number 1614-82/18, of the 11th of October, 1991, regulating the procedure of vehicles entering the town of Vukovar with food and journalists and the treatment of women, children, and the elderly." We don't have this order among our documents, at least I didn't manage to find it except for this entry in the war diary. Tell me, then, do you remember, after this document, what the procedure was in relation to these matters, especially this treatment of women, children, and the elderly? Why are younger men not referred to there, if I can put it that way?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already spoken about that. I talked about it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you just slow down a bit, please.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we came to the area of Vukovar, I personally expected - and I believe that many other officers did, too --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, I really have to interrupt you. I keep telling you: Please slow down. Speak two times slower than you are speaking now.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I and, I believe, many other officers were expecting that when our units came to Vukovar that people would accept us as their own soldiers and make it possible for us to carry out our task of disarming the paramilitary formations, and for people to live a normal life in that town. However, the opposite happened. When fierce combat started, if I can put it that way, all of a sudden, many civilians started cropping up - women, children, and so on. As far as I can remember, this order regulated the following: that all women, children, and elderly persons and persons who are unfit for carrying out combat, if I can put it that way, should be allowed to leave the combat zone and that they should be evacuated to the Red Cross in Sid. Whoever wished to remain at their homes could stay on. We wouldn't touch them. Why men are not being referred to, well, the reason for that is that all able-bodied military-aged men should stay on and help the units of the JNA carry out these tasks. That is how I understood that order, as far as I can remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are going to look at one of your reports later on. What about the feeling of the local population? Did they want to actively participate in combat, in your view?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The prevailing feelings differed or varied. Many of these local people were sometimes even bothered, if I can put it that way, by the Yugoslav Peoples' Army, because they called for discipline, law and order, and some say that they minded the fact that we wore the red five-pointed star. So feelings varied, as I said to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we are going to look at something else. It seems that Mr. Theunens and the Prosecutor were particularly interested in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The page I would like to display now on the screen is 0293-5466. The English version, page 30; B/C/S version is 33. That is the entry of the 21st of October, at 1630 hours. Perhaps we can zoom in on the lower part.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, what it says here is: "On the 21st of October, at 1630 hours, Major Veselin Sljivancanin informed General Panic that, during the course of the day, he corrected artillery fire in the Mitnica sector at about 1300 hours." What can you tell us about this entry? Just please speak slower and try to be as brief as possible.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said in my reports, too, that as I was touring the units, and as I spoke to individuals, I came to learn that artillery units of the 1st Military District are not targeting precisely, and they're even hitting the positions of our own soldiers. I informed my commander, Colonel Mrksic, about that, too. Mrksic intervened with the command of the 1st Military District, but individuals proclaimed me to be too emotional, that is to say, individuals from the command of the 1st Military District, and that I was taking this in a way, well, that was not correct. Again, I remained at these positions and I spent the night with the unit commanded by Witness P01, and I experienced something like that. And, again, I asked the commander to have attention drawn to this and to prevent things like that from happening. General Panic personally wanted to speak to me; he was the commander of the Military District. I explain what this was all about. He had his doubts regarding my report, but he said that he would send the chief of artillery to see for himself whether that was true. He came on this day, as stated here, the chief of artillery - I remember his name was Colonel Grce - to the commander. The commander is present there, too. We informed him about the situation and it was agreed that the colonel should go with me to Vukovar, that I should select a target, and that we should check whether that is true. Colonel Grce gave orders to some artillery officers who I don't know - I cannot remember all names now - to go with me, and we chose the area of the observation point of Vinarija, in Vukovar. That is the building from which Mitnica can be seen the best, because this is a plain, this is where it is flat. At a lower level of Mitnica, there was the fortification from where they were firing towards Dudinjak. I asked the colonel to have artillery commanded from there, as this is done through communications equipment, and that his observers should see where the shells will fall. He took all his people along - his signalmen, his other soldiers - and he did this at Vinarija. They targeted individual targets. I think they used howitzers of 122 millimetres and then howitzers of 155. And to keep this as short as possible, not a single artillery piece hit its target. They really went off the mark, even up to 400 metres. From there, we went to the firing positions of the units. He took me in his vehicle to where these units were deployed to check why this was not done right. Since it was raining heavily at the time - and it was a flat land; there is mud - the units were dug in the ground and their ammunition got wet due to the heavy rain. And it was concluded that it was their gunpowder charges that got damp and that that is why these mistakes were made. This was the professional answer of the artillery organs. We returned to the command post. We told the commander about this and they understood that I was right. The commander ordered me to report personally, then, to General Panic and to tell him that what I had talked about was true. And that is why this entry was made in the war diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why did you, as a security organ, take such an active part in this matter? Why did it matter so much to you?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my answer, I said that officers from the command of the 1st Military District doubted the veracity of the information that I had provided. I was in a situation where I had to justify such information and prove that it was accurate. There is no greater task for a security organ than to ascertain whether an activity was the work of the enemy, if it turns out that your own forces are killing each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That wraps up the issue of the war log. Now we'll be moving on to the events described in the indictment, those that get the greatest amount of attention during this trial. Is there any reason why you remember the 18th [as interpreted] of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a method, a security method, that I used at the time and this method is called "misinformation."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correction: I said the 17th of November and the transcript reflects the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll talk about that later but now we're talking about the 17th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, it seems you are trying to get me to say something specific, and this is something that we discussed. Yes, I remember this date really well because I used a method of security work called "spreading misinformation." That's what the method was called. I was criticised for this but that's what I did. What am I talking about? I said before that, during the lifting of the siege of the barracks, we had captured very few paramilitaries. Throughout this entire time, it didn't go beyond a mere 20 for as long as a month, 20 people captured. Based on interviews that I conducted with those people, I learned, "Whenever we can, we watched TV Belgrade most of all, because TV Belgrade conveys information in an accurate manner without trying to hide anything. TV Zagreb is something we no longer watch because they are trying to manipulate us and are lying to us." I said, "What sort of information?" and they said, "TV Belgrade shows exactly the footage which shows the position of your forces and we know exactly the street in which your forces are deployed or how far you got, that sort of thing." As we had spent quite some time in the area, my desire was to complete the mission as soon as possible and for Vukovar to be a free town. This was Sunday, the 17th. On Sundays, there was one television centre in Yugoslavia which aired TV news for the whole territory of the former Yugoslavia. It was that afternoon, the afternoon of the 17th, that I was at Milovo Brdo with Major Tesic. On the preceding days, Major Tesic was in the area all the time. Major Tesic told me that a TV crew from Novi Sad was asking to speak to me. Bearing in mind what I had been told by the captured members of the Croat paramilitary units, I advised the officers to not take all their teams to the front line because then everybody watching the TV would know our positions. Nonetheless, Tesic went there to tell the crew that I would not be making a statement and that I wasn't in the area. However, they were persistent and eventually I decided to make a statement. They told me they were a crew preparing the 1930 hours TV news to be aired throughout the former Yugoslavia. Having remembered what I had been told by the captured paramilitaries, I stated, among other things, that Vukovar had been liberated. So this is a piece of misinformation that I tried to have circulated just to see what the Croat paramilitaries would do next. There are other things that I said in that particular declaration, and I can't remember everything that I said. Later, I realised that I had made a mistake because I had failed to confer with my commander for him to approve this method. At about 1800 hours, I was back at the command post and I reported to the commander. I told him about making such and such a statement for TV Novi Sad and what my intention was. He criticised me, but there was no changing what had happened. I hoped that this would eventually not be aired. So that evening, at about 8.00, we watched the Novi Sad TV news and the supplement and they aired my statement as it was. The first name they put on the screen was "Major Veselin Sljivovcanin." They twisted my name around, but my name had never previously appeared on a TV screen, so they didn't know. Later on, at about 9.00 that evening, I had this radio and I got a call over this radio from one of the Croatian paramilitaries, asking to speak to "Major Sljivovcanin." That's why I remember this happening because they didn't get my name right. I told the commander about this, and straight after we received a call at the switchboard of our signals unit and they said that they wished to discuss the possibility of a surrender. We conferred briefly and took this for some sort of deception, a ploy, because our own forces at the front line were meager at the time, because many people had been wounded. The reservists had left. We had sent away some of the volunteers that we believed could no longer stay at the front line. As a result, Colonel Mrksic ordered me not to talk to anyone anymore. He also said that all conversations would be conducted through the signals switchboard at the brigade's headquarters and he said that he would be conducting any future conversations or any other officers present there. So I simply switched my radio off. I know that throughout that night members of the Croat paramilitary forces called, because the next morning I received a report to that effect. I know it was at about 1.00 or 2.00, early in the morning, and Mr. Mrksic scheduled a meeting for the following morning, early morning hours, at about 8.00 or 9.00, a meeting with Marin Vidic, Bili. I listened to his conversation with Marin Vidic, Bili, over the radio the following morning and the conditions that he imposed. The morning of the 18th of November, 1991, he gave Colonel Pavkovic the responsibility of using our eavesdropping equipment to talk to the Mitnica commander about their surrender, which Pavkovic eventually did at about 9.00. I'm talking about the morning of the 18th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the conversation between Colonel Mrksic and Mr. Marin Vidic, Bili? You said you were there when they talked. What exactly did Mrksic say on that occasion? What were the conditions that he specified, the conditions for their surrender, insofar as that was discussed at all? And where exactly was Mr. Vidic located, in which area?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Pavkovic had returned to the command post of the Guards Brigade, if I remember correctly, at about 9.00. It may have been between 9.00 and 10.00. From this place where we had our eavesdropping equipment, which was a place between Negoslavci and Ovcara, he said he had got in touch with the forces at Mitnica and that they were now willing to surrender. As far as I was able to memorise his words, Mr. Mrksic dictated to Mr. Vidic the terms of surrender. I think Vidic was speaking from the hospital area. That was outside our own area and we still said that we would accept their surrender under the following terms: All of the armed paramilitaries should go to the stadium known as Rupe, and I can show you the location of the stadium on the map. He said they should lay down their weapons and he would guarantee safety for those of the JNA men who would be checking that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who is "he"?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean Marin Vidic. As far as I know, Marin Vidic was not able to make that promise off the bat, in terms of being able to control the whole situation, but he did say that he would get back to us later, as soon as he had agreed everything with those people who were about to surrender. However, I don't think he called again to talk about the surrender or the terms of surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can I therefore conclude, without leading, that these were two separate instances of people surrendering? Are we talking about the same forces surrendering from the same area or were these two different groups surrendering?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were two totally different locations. On the one hand, there were the forces at Mitnica under the command of Dmitar Karaula, and on the other, the forces in the general hospital area. I don't know who their commander was. At this point in time, those two groups were not in touch. Mitnica was in the area of operations of the Guards Brigade, whereas the hospital, at that time, was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened later? Let's talk about the Mitnica group first, the Mitnica evacuation. Do you know what happened next, that morning? And then we'll see what you did.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Having conducted these talks, Commander Mrksic issued precise assignments to the officers, or rather, the unit commanders, tasking Colonel Pavkovic and Colonel Marko Maric, who was the assistant for moral guidance, with going there and negotiating the surrender at Mitnica. He tasked me, or rather gave me a task, with tracking down the ICRC people because I was the one liaising with them, and to allow them to go and attend the surrender negotiations. He also said that I should make sure, through the press centre, for journalists to be there and to wait there until all the terms had been agreed, all the terms of the surrender, and to keep them from straying and wandering all along the front line. If any international organisation arrived or their representatives, he said I should welcome them and show them whatever I could. That was as far as he went.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would now like to see a clip. This is V0000686. We have a brief portion of this video in evidence already when we heard witness Sarlota Foro. I think it's about 17 minutes long, this particular clip. I don't want us to watch the whole thing. There's a transcript for this which also comprises the Mitnica surrender negotiations and the participants. It is 3D060023. I would like us now to see the rather short portion of this video, and then if the OTP agree, we don't need to see the entire clip. Afterwards we'll be tendering it. We can have a look and see what Mr. Sljivancanin has to say about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're at 00:32. We can just let it run on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, what do you think this is?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can see in this video is an ICRC vehicle, and as far as I can tell, this is the road leading from Negoslavci to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's just move along and then we can comment as we go along. Now we are at 01:15.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the house at Ovcara where, for a while, there was the command post of the commander of the 20th Partisan Brigade. Later on, it was the command post of a unit from the 80th Motorised Brigade, although I didn't know anything more specific about that brigade at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We're at 01:45.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Mr. Borsinger

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we pause there for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this frame, you can see Mr. Borsinger, Colonel Nebojsa Pavkovic. This arrow is a helmet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This person on the right; right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the person wearing the camouflage uniform is Major Milorad Stupar, the commander of the 3rd Assault Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He's on the left; right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're at 04:29.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, do you know what's going on here in this frame?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This frame, you can see Mr. Borsinger and Major Stupar meeting representatives of the Croatian paramilitary forces. This gentleman with the hand-held radio is someone I met when they were surrendering their weapons and I allowed him to keep some souvenirs that he had on him at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is his name?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dmitar Karaula.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're at 07:15.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about this? Do you recognise this area?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In passing, yes. I have a passing familiarity with this area. This, I think, is a part of Mitnica known as Vucedol, buildings and houses there, flanking the Vukovar-Sotin road.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At 7:45, who do we see here?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Colonel Pavkovic, the representatives of the Croatian paramilitary units. As far as I can see, Major Skoric is there, too, but I'm not certain because the image is not clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we pause there, please. From this point on, we have the negotiations and that takes quite some time. If Mr. Moore agrees and if the Chamber agrees, we might tender this now and avoid looking at the whole thing because it's quite lengthy. Previously though, I would like to ask Mr. Sljivancanin a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, did you attend these negotiations at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at any point. At this time I was elsewhere with the European monitors, in Velepromet and at Milovo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We have no objection to this being made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 831, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall the transcript be assigned a separate number, 3D060023, that one?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The transcript will become Exhibit 832, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now take our second break, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at 20 minutes to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, we heard your testimony to the effect that you did not take part in those negotiations and I shall add "at Vucedol," to be precise, with the Mitnica group, that is. Did you in any way see Mr. Borsinger that morning, and when was that, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That morning, the 18th of November, 1991, I saw Mr. Borsinger in the village of Negoslavci, around 1000 hours, where he came after having been called and reminded to come to negotiations, and after that I introduced him to Colonel Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at Exhibit 140 again, a video clip which was tendered during the testimony of Mr. van Lynden, I believe. I'm not quite sure. Can we take a look at that exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, where was this, and what is it that we've just seen?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of this footage, the person exiting the military jeep is the commander of the traffic transport company from the 1st Battalion of the military police, Dane Krajisnik. He went to fetch Mr. Borsinger. Actually, I sent several people to seek him out, to look for him. And he brought him to Negoslavci and I introduced him to Mr. Pavkovic, and I asked him to be present at the negotiations regarding the surrender of Mitnica. And all this was ordered by Colonel Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not to be leading, what we say relative to the previous video footage, when you went to Mitnica, I suppose that this was before.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was before. You can see now that the column was setting off towards -- for Mitnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any encounters that morning, that day, with the press?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said, when Colonel Mrksic assigned -- when I talked about the assignments given us by Colonel Mrksic, that morning, on the 18th, around 9.00, I asked Captain Zvorcan to assemble the journalists in the press centre so that I could ask them not to go to the front line and to wait there, and tell them that we would be informing them if we reached an agreement. I gave them some brief information, the information that I had at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will now move on. What happened afterwards? Whom did you see after that?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that I met with representatives of the European Monitors, and I remember that a gentleman was there whom I recognised because he took the stand here, Mr. Kypr and Mr. Schou, whom you can see in the footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now we shall take a look at that clip, also. How long did they stay there in Negoslavci, and what happened afterwards, during the morning?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, we had some sort of an agreement in this house, in the village of Negoslavci, where the press centre was, or in the house right next to it; I'm not quite sure at this point. But perhaps I could point to it on the clip. I informed them, on behalf of the command of the Motorised Guards Brigade, what the units of the Guards Brigade were doing currently regarding the agreements to be -- the negotiations to be conducted at Mitnica. And I told them that very many civilians were coming to Velepromet. They said that they wanted to see that and to see what could be shown to them in other parts of Vukovar also. Mr. Kypr, if I am saying his name right, requested for me to sign my name, in my hand, in his notebook because he had a problem remembering names, because he wanted to have my name exactly so that he would know whom he had talked to. And I did that; I wrote my name in his notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have Exhibit 314 on the screen for one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until it comes, can I just add: They always asked that no journalists attend our talks. So I had to address the journalists that morning and to order them, actually, not to be present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we zoom in on the central portion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is in my handwriting. It says "Major Veselin Sljivancanin." I was never ashamed of my first or last name or of anything that I was doing for my country, for my people, although I knew that they were people who were engaged in intelligence activities, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We shall take a look at the video. Let me just see.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened afterwards? No. First tell me, had you ever, before that day, met Mr. Kypr and people from the European Monitoring Mission?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, before that, as I said, I had had two or three encounters, and I recognised Mr. Schou from the encounter that we had at elevation point 102 on the 19th of October, as shown here. When we greeted each other in the morning, I told him that I knew him and he told me that he had never set eyes on me before in his life and that that was the first time. Now, as regards Mr. Kypr, I don't know whether that is the case. I cannot remember the other details. You were asking me what happened afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just wait a bit. Let us take a look at the video clip. Please do slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we are going to take a look at video clip V000625, is the reference to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You can comment now, Mr. Sljivancanin. You can comment on the video footage.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from what I can recognise, this is the vehicle of the European Monitoring Mission, the kind they used to come to the sector of our unit, and this is the village of Negoslavci. This is them. This is the house where we had that first meeting on the morning of the 18th, so the meeting on the 18th, in the morning, and as far as I can recall, it was sometime around 10.00 in the morning. The liaison officer who arrived there on behalf of the SSNO met them, saw them. This is the actual venue of the meeting. The gentleman asked me to send away the press. This here is Captain Zvorcan at the press centre. I asked the journalists -- this is me asking the journalists to leave because the European Monitoring Mission representatives asked me to do that. And throughout their stay in our zone, I always endeavored. And that was also the position of the commander, to make it possible for them to do their job and to accommodate their requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please do not comment on this part of the video. Let us hear what you have to say.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] We agreed with the gentleman from the European Community on our further work plans. They accepted what I said; I accepted what they said. So I should like to tell all the citizens and all the people, We are going to pursue our mission alone without the journalists. When the time for journalists come, we shall say so, so let us not make any problems. Please be so kind as to appreciate this, because we are treating you fair and correctly. And we will be informing you about everything which is important so that you can note it down. The minute we finish our work, if it happens -- if it is solved, as I told you this morning, at that level, you will be informed of everything we said. And please respect what I've just told you. Radojica, it is your duty. Don't let the journalists follow me."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we tender this document into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 833, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I shall not comment on this or you shall not comment on this, what you just told us a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened afterwards? Where did you go from Negoslavci, later that day?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said, first, they asked me to take me to Velepromet where a large number of civilians were assembling, as well as people who were coming from the centre of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who asked you to do that?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The European monitors did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: So we were there at Velepromet. After that, they insisted that I take them to a place from which one could see the disposition of the events currently going on in Vukovar, so I took them to Milovo Brdo, Milovo hill. Fighting was still going on in the centre of Vukovar; one could hear intermittent fire. They wanted to know where the Vukovar Hospital was, so from Milovo Brdo - and this can be measured on the topographic map which we have here - one can see the roof of the Vukovar Hospital across the River Vuka, a kilometre and a half or a bit more distance, as the crow flies. Also, the area the Mitnica could be seen. They saw it and they expressed the desire to return and to talk to these civilians who had assembled at Velepromet. They were introduced to the manager of this holding centre, this reception centre, Ljubinko Stojanovic. And sometime that day, perhaps after 1400 hours, I said good-bye to them and they went on their own business. They also talked to those civilians and they said that they were supposed to return to Belgrade and submit a report. This is what they said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have Exhibit 339 on the screen for one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we were still talking, I did not know, I had no information, about the outcome of the talks at Mitnica. And I also explained to them to which point did the border of the zone of the Guards Brigade stretch, and that the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, the interpreter did not hear the end of the answer because of the overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see the timing of this visit. Do you agree that around this period, this visit actually took place around this time period? And were you with them all the time?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it says here in the last paragraph that the last talk with the refugees was around 1445 until 1530 hours and that they left Vukovar at 1530 hours. I believe that these people followed this meticulously. And as far as my memory serves me, I know that I talked with Captain Karanfilov about the surrender in Mitnica in Negoslavci between 15 and 14 hours, if I remember, plus or minus 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you a simple question: Were you with them until they left, all the time? So were you with them until they left Negoslavci, all the time?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I said good-bye to them at Velepromet, after we had returned from Milovo Brdo. Now, did they or did they not stay there for another half hour or not, I really can't say. The officers from the military police and the liaison officers stayed with them. I didn't follow them throughout that period. They said that they would be returning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please slow down. What happened then, Mr. Sljivancanin? What were your activities after that?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, I came to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just slower, please.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came to Negoslavci, to the house where I was staying. Probably I had some lunch as well. And I called Captain Borce Karanfilov, since I had assigned him to go to Mitnica with Colonel Pavkovic, to give me results about the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the reason for Captain Karanfilov to go to Mitnica? What was this task that you gave him?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The primary task that I gave him then was to be Colonel Pavkovic's security because Colonel Pavkovic asked me for that. His task was not to take part in the negotiations. The captain then informed me that the negotiations had ended and that the commander of the paramilitary forces of Croatia had accepted a surrender, and that the surrender would take place in the afternoon hours. I think, as I remember it now, when I came to Mitnica then, it was sometime after 1500 or 1600 hours. At that time I found some people who were surrendering their weapons. The units that were doing this were doing this in an organised manner. And I know then that the captain asked me about this gentleman, who I recognised in the photograph before, whether some of his personal belongings can be left, whether he could keep them as a memento. And I said, "Don't do anything to the man," because I looked upon him then as a fair person, a fair fighter, and I said that they should not take anything from him except for weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you find out - and if so, when? - what was supposed to happen to these people once they surrendered their weapons? Who made the decision? What was the plan? What happened to this Mitnica group? When did you find out about that, and what was it that you found out?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: These people who surrendered were no longer of interest to the security organs because they, themselves, laid down their weapons and accepted that they were members of the paramilitary forces of Croatia. As for the decision on where they would be taken afterwards and where they would be put up, as far as I know, this decision was made by Colonel Mrksic. And he gave tasks to commanders in the zone as to what would be their treatment later on, where they would be taken, and so on. Through some talks with my security organs, I was asking them whether they could give us information about where their arms depots were, whether there were any left, were there any minefields left, and did they know anything that they could tell us so that people could not be hurt by explosive devices that were left behind. May I also say that in these talks, they were very fair and that they said a great many things. I was interested in this work afterwards in the area of Mitnica itself and in assisting the civilian population and in taking care of these people. I wanted to check whether, perhaps, among this civilian population there was somebody who was hiding, somebody who had belonged to the paramilitary formations and had committed a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How much time did you spend there at Mitnica, if I can put it that way? Where were you, specifically, the place? I mean Mitnica is a broad concept.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the area of Vucedol, as I said first, and, for the most part, people from the area of Mitnica came to Vucedol. It was twilight; it was almost dark by then, just before nightfall. Well, before that, perhaps I said already that I informed the brigade command that there were many civilians there and that vehicles should be sent for their evacuation. They reacted quickly and there are entries in the war log of the Guards Brigade about that. I believe that this was regulated through command channels, that it was said then that, for the first time, in addition to the fact that the civilians could go to the Red Cross, to Sid, that those civilians who wanted to go to Croatia could go to Croatia, and that the army would provide transportation for that. So there were two groups of civilians; one group of civilians that were supposed to go to Sid and the other group that were supposed to go to Croatia, in that area the Vucedol. As for these civilians, most of them wanted to go to Croatia, a vast majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many were there, in your estimate?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my estimate, at that time at Mitnica, there were over 4.000 civilians. And I was there with my assistant, Major Ljubisa Vukasinovic. We were moving about through these civilians, and I said to him at one point, "You see, Ljubisa, how few soldiers are securing these civilians?" There were up to 30 of them. "And look at the masses of these people. And if they knew that there were only 30 of us here, if they were to take sticks, they could beat us all." And I said, "That is why you will now understand why resistance was so strong." At that point a messenger came, a soldier who was looking for me, and he introduced himself, saying that he was coming from the command of the brigade and that he was bringing me a telegram. I took that envelope; I opened it. It was probably a coded telegram. And then the signal centre wrote the -- wrote this in hand. I remember the content of the telegram very well. "Around 2.000 of our soldiers and officers are in Croat prisons. What should be done is to bring in as many perpetrators of crimes as possible in order to carry out an exchange," signed Major General Aca Vasiljevic. I looked at this telegram for a while and I handed it over to Major Vukasinovic, and I said, "Have a look at this telegram." He read the telegram. I put it in my notebook. And that evening, both I and Major Vukasinovic stayed in the area of Vucedol some time, until 2300 hours, 11.00 p.m., if I can put it that way, where we were trying to help the other soldiers and officers to have the civilians board the buses, the vehicles assigned by the Yugoslav Peoples' Army, and that we help; that they be divided into these two groups. There were certainly officers who were assigned, who would be in charge of which convoy, and that they be sent to where they wanted to go. At the same time we were interviewing individuals to see whether there were any perpetrators of crimes among them. We were assisted in this by the members of the Territorial Defence of Vukovar who knew people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On that day, did you go to Ovcara? On that day, on that evening.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that evening, to the best of my recollection, I came to the area of Ovcara with a convoy of buses. The civilians from Vucedol were on these buses, those who wanted to go to Croatia. A group came with this convoy, a group of civilian vehicles and vehicles like tractors, too. The convoy stopped at Ovcara. This is where we were met by an officer who I didn't know at the time. He introduced himself as being from the 80th Motorised Brigade. And he said that his troops were now in the area of Ovcara and that they were in charge of security. I asked that all these vehicles, civilian vehicles, tractors, et cetera, be parked on a field, a meadow. And he told these civilians that if they wanted to leave this area, they could board the buses and that their wishes would be met, as I said, these different groups; and that the motor vehicles had to stay there; and that people could not take private vehicles for the sake of security and safety; and that these vehicles would then be transported to Velepromet, to the reception centre there, under the control of the Territorial Defence of the town of Vukovar. I certainly remember this very well. It was between 2300 hours and 1.00, after midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This officer that you described just now, did you recognise him later?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite a bit later. When I went to work at the Centre of Military Schools, and through a conversation, I found out --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Don't say any names.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that he has the name that he has and -- because I recognised him at the Centre of Military Schools. And he was a witness here and I don't know exactly the pseudonym under which he testified here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move into private session for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened to these civilians that evening? What happened that evening? You heard the testimony of Sarlota Foro. Did that jog your memory? Do you remember any details?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, many of the testimonies I heard here jogged my memory. And I must say that in that part of the statement regarding Ovcara in that some territorials asked me something, that they were indicating some persons with their fingers, saying that they were crime suspects, and I said that they should board the buses and I don't want to separate them from their families. Somebody else testified about this. And I confirm that the time could have been, as she put it, Ms. Foro. And I know that the leader of that convoy was Major Skoric, because he reported for that duty; and that the column -- the convoy was followed by the transport police from the 1st Battalion of the military police; and that the commander of that security, that escort - I remember that very profoundly - it was Captain Jankovic, who was deputy commander of a company in the traffic police. When I came to Negoslavci, I found out that this convoy was supposed to leave that evening, immediately, because we did not have any space to put people up and we didn't want anybody to freeze out there. And I think that it was on the highway towards Sid, going to Zagreb, and then they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since we heard testimony before this Court that that night, in Ovcara, members of the Mitnica group were there in that hangar, did you see them? Did you go to the hangar? And in that respect, did you have any contacts?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for these people who had surrendered and who had confessed that they had fired and that they used weapons, we did not do anything vis-a-vis them, because our orders were to send these people immediately to Sremska Mitrovica and that there were the right organs there that would deal with these people. And Captain Borce Karanfilov was the person I assigned to see to them, and he informed me on the 19th that these people had gone to Sremska Mitrovica. I never went to that hangar and I did not know where they were put up that night. The first time I saw this hangar was here, in pictures. Had you asked me before about that, the only thing I know in Ovcara is that yellow house, where the command was. And I know this yellow house more from my previous contacts with the commander of the 20th Partisan Brigade, Mr. Slobodan Misovic, Lieutenant Colonel Slobodan Micevic, because he is a Montenegrin. He comes from the same area that I come from. I came to him, to ask him for help, but unfortunately he did not help me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As for what you witnessed in Ovcara on the evening of the 18th, that is to say, this dialogue with Foro, with the civilians, the territorials, where was this happening, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where was this happening? The road from Vucedol leads on to Ovcara, and then there's a flat area, a green area. So it's to the right of the Vucedol-Ovcara road, looking in the direction of Ovcara. It was night-time, however, and I didn't notice any buildings or anything. I know that it was night-time and it was all flat. It's to the right, if you head from Vucedol towards Ovcara. I didn't notice any buildings nearby, near this flat area, flat stretch, to the extent that my perception was accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were any of your security people there with you at Ovcara that evening?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, that whole evening or that afternoon, there was Major Ljubisa Vukasinovic who was with me throughout. It's not just based on my recollection. I'm actually certain that he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say you were there late at night. Is there anything else etched in your mind about the 18th, or do you think we can move on to the next day?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: One thing that I do remember is late at night, it was past midnight, I arrived at the Guards Brigade headquarters in Negoslavci. I told them about everything that had occurred at Ovcara, and I was tired. I received the order at this time to go to a meeting at Colonel Mrksic's at about 7.00 the following morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We're listening. What happens next?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next morning I went and reported to the colonel. He informed us, the officers from the core command -- and I think Colonel Pavkovic was there, too, but I can't be certain. What I'm certain about is the presence of the Chief of Staff, the assistant commander for moral guidance. I'm not sure about the assistant commander for logistics. There was someone from the operations and training organ, and he gave a specific assignment to me. He said a high-ranking delegation, led by Mr. Cyrus Vance, would be visiting our unit and their arrival was expected about 10.00 that same day. He said I should do everything necessary to welcome them as they entered the village of Negoslavci. He said we should take them to the command post and that all of us assistant commanders would be attending the meeting that the colonel would be holding with that particular delegation. That's what I remember. After this I handed out assignments to my own security assistants. I told them what each of them would be doing. I think I pointed out with particular attention to Captain Karanfilov to see if those men who had been disarmed at Mitnica had been sent to Sremska Mitrovica and to report back to me about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about this: From your own area of operations, were any prisoners ever sent to Sremska Mitrovica, or was this the first time? Or perhaps you've talked about it already, so my apologies in that case.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, no prisoners had ever been sent to Sremska Mitrovica up until this point in time. We had been taking very few prisoners and we'd never seen this coming. We thought we would be taking, at most, two or three prisoners, and this was the first time an order ever came for us to send prisoners to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's hear about Mr. Vance's visit now. We've all heard evidence before this Court by Mr. Okun, but before any specific questions, could you please give us your own account of Mr. Vance's visit. And what exactly was your role?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remembered that the battalion commander, the 1st Battalion of the military police, having received approval from the brigade commander, assigned a police patrol with a vehicle. This patrol met the convoy carrying Mr. Vance. We then took them to the command post to see the commander. The commander was waiting for them outside the building. We went straight into a room and we sat down. The commander had a map of the town of Vukovar, a huge sketch, if you like, and he told the Vance delegation everything that they wanted to know about. I think the briefing went on until about 11.00. It had been announced, or at least that's what the commander had told us, that this delegation would not be staying in our area past 2.00 that day, unless I'm mistaken, and I may have forgotten, but I believe this to have been the case. After this final meeting, Mr. Vance expressed a desire to go to Vukovar himself, to see for himself what things were like there. The delegation arrived outside the Secretariat for All People's Defence. Accompanying Mr. Vance was my own technical assistant for security-related issues, the Chief of Staff of the cabinet of the Federal Secretary for All People's Defence, Lieutenant Colonel Dragoljub Djukic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Chief of security of the cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Dragoljub Djukic, is that the person who signed all these documents that we've been looking at this morning?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, that's the very person.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: With him was the chief of the liaison department, who was in charge of liaising with international military representatives, Colonel Pero Stojic. I know about those two being there for a fact. There may have been other officers there, too, but that escapes me right now. I can hardly be expected to remember every one. So, once Mr. Vance had expressed this desire to go and visit Vukovar, Colonel Mrksic called my name, he said, "Major Sljivancanin, now you will go with the delegation. Take Mr. Vance to all the safe places for him to be able to see whatever he wishes to see." I carried out this assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During their visit, or upon their arrival in Negoslavci and later, until the very end of their visit, were there any journalists accompanying you?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout all this time, from Vance's arrival to the time he left, there was a large group of journalists tagging along and they went everywhere in Vukovar. There were two journalist crews that drove in with Mr. Vance in the same vehicle, and they never stayed away from this delegation. They were always with them; they always stayed close.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So what exactly do you remember? Where did you go? What did you see?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We drove in an APC belonging to the military police, belonging to the 1st Battalion of the military police. I was in this APC together with Mr. Vance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember anyone else from that APC?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember there was the liaison officer and Colonel Pavkovic or Pero Stojic may have been in that same APC. It was either of those two. But there was room enough to hold eight soldiers, but we didn't want it to be too crowded. I'm sure that Mr. Vance was there; the liaison officer was there because he was interpreting our conversation; and there was either one of these two officers that I mentioned. The first place we arrived at was the Vukovar barracks because he wanted to be shown the barracks, so we did. During our conversation, I talked to Mr. Vance about the partisans in World War II. We also talked about the partisans entering the city in Trieste, in Italy, in World War II and about the arrival of the American forces in that city. I was glad that we had been allies in World War II and I think he was glad about this, too, at least that was the feeling I had. After that, I took him and the entire delegation to the Velepromet facility where there were a large number of refugees. We stayed at Velepromet for quite some time. Vance spoke to some of the refugees and some of the other people there. We weren't trying to stage anything for this high-ranking delegation from an important country. At one point he asked if we could go and see the Vukovar Hospital. I explained to him that the hospital was in an area that was under the control of a different unit. But having previously been advised by General Vasiljevic, without taking the chief of the general staff with nobody's approval, I replied to Mr. Vance that I wasn't authorised to take anybody there, including him. It wasn't safe. There was still fighting in downtown Vukovar, at least according to my information, such information as was available to me at the time. I simply couldn't meet this request. I also knew that many of the areas were still booby-trapped. There was something said by the leader of that team. I think it was either Pero Stojic or Colonel Pavkovic. They said they were in no position to take Vance anywhere outside our own area. I tried to explain and I told him how I saw things, that I was in no position to take him anywhere outside our own area. He then wanted to be taken somewhere else from where he had a view of Vukovar. I then took him to Milovo Brdo, and it was from there that Mr. Vance surveyed the Vukovar Hospital. There, you had a view of the roof, the hospital roof from there. We explained everything about the bridges and the Vuka River, because that was within sight. And then I said this: If he still wanted to see a hospital, there was a hospital over in Negoslavci and maybe it was a good idea for him to go and visit that one. He replied that it was late. He said he ought to make it to a different meeting in Zagreb that same day, and they still had to drive back to Belgrade so there would be no time left for them. I said, and I remember clearly what I said at the time: "Mr. Vance, today we have declared a holiday for us and our soldiers, because we are greatly honoured that you, as a high-ranking international politician and a representative of a great power, a power that was our ally in World War II, are here to visit our country and our unit. You should go and see that hospital, since at this point in time that is probably the most humane hospital anywhere, worldwide." He said, "How come? What exactly do you mean?" I replied, "Because, as we speak, our young soldiers and officers are receiving treatment there, who, through no fault of their own, have been wounded or killed. Everybody, the entire population of this area, is receiving treatment there as we speak. Go there and see for yourself that our doctors are extending the best possible care also to those paramilitaries who had, until not such a long time ago, been firing at those same soldiers that are being treated there now."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How long did he stay there for?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just let me wrap this up. And then Mr. Vance said that he did, indeed, want to go there and see the hospital. So off we went to Negoslavci. I thought he would only stay for a brief while, but when he realised what I had been talking about, what I had been telling him about, I think the delegation must have stayed at the hospital for at least half an hour, maybe even up to one hour. And there was a gentleman who was with him who was telling everybody else to take notes, to write down what they saw around them, inside the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did you part ways, eventually?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's another detail that I have to mention. I'm sorry, but this is really important. On the road between Milovo Brdo and Negoslavci, inside the APC, at one point in time Mr. Vance asked me, "Major, sir, will your unit launch an attack on Osijek?" That was a mere hour after this previous assignment had been accomplished. I was moved, in a way, by his question. I said, "Mr. Vance, my unit will always follow orders issued by our Superior Command, but I see no reason for us to attack Osijek since it is a town in our own country." And then he replied, "Major, sir, do you know about the ethnic make-up of that town?" and I said, "Mr. Vance, I really don't know. I'm not familiar with the ethnic make-up of Osijek." He said, "73 per cent of the town's population are Croats, roughly speaking, and those same Croats see you, the JNA, as an occupation army, as an aggressor." I fell silent and I was simply speechless. I had no answer to that one. I wanted to change the subject because I really couldn't bring myself to believe that all those people with whom we had happily coexisted until not such a long time ago now saw us as an occupation army and as an aggressor. So we proceeded along our way. The hospital visit was now over, and we parted ways on very friendly terms. Mr. Vance thanked us and said something to the effect that he was really glad to have visited a JNA unit like this one, but that he wasn't really happy about the timing of his visit, since this was a very unfortunate time, a miserable time. He said everything would be done within their power to stop interethnic clashes in Yugoslavia. He said his impression at the time was that we had not concealed anything from him. He believed we had shown him the situation for what it was. Should there be another opportunity, he said he would make sure to return and visit our unit again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did you learn that members of your unit had reached the hospital? When did you first hear that they had reached the hospital? And when you heard, what exactly was the information about? When did they get there?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I heard of this was that same day, the afternoon of that same day. It was past 2.00 p.m., when Vance had already left our area, and then I went back to Colonel Mrksic's command post. He personally shared this with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You saw a document during the proceedings. It has been exhibited. It's a report to the effect that members of the Guards Brigade's operations group reached the hospital at about 11.00. So you heard they had reached the hospital. What were you told about the timing of their arrival, and is that consistent with the report?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember this very clearly. Once my assignment with Mr. Vance had been completed, I was off to the command post to inform the commander about the fact that the delegation had left the area under the control of our unit. As far as I remember, Colonel Mrksic told me this: "Fine, did everything go smoothly?" I said, "Yes." And he said, "The units of the 1st Motorised Battalion had crossed the Vuka River and had entered the police station area and the hospital area. I had the hospital director here to come and talk to me and I promised that we would be sending medicines, food, water and all the other necessities, to the hospital. As you are the one who is permanently in touch with the representatives of all these international organisations, track them down for me and see if they can secure an amount of medicines to be sent to the hospital. In addition to this, you need to go to the hospital with these representatives. You need to verify the security reports that I had received about what was really going on over there. We want to know more about our own missing soldiers. As far as I remember, he also mentioned that commander that you were looking for all the time, the commander of the Croatian forces. See if you can go there and meet him."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll probably have to deal with this tomorrow, about Mr. Vance's visit. Just two questions left for today. You've heard Mr. Okun's testimony live, haven't you? During that entire visit, did you have a slanging match, a shouting match, at any time with Mr. Vance? And the other thing we heard: Did you, at any point, train your rifle at him or physically stand in his way and keep him from visiting the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, when I heard that evidence, there was a turmoil in my head and the entire courtroom seemed to be spinning. I welcomed Mr. Vance as a well-respected gentleman and a high-ranking politician, a senior politician, if you like. I was relatively young at the time, myself. Sometimes I want to, perhaps, raise my voice and someone may as well call that yelling or shouting, but that is just my normal tone of voice. That is how I see it, be that as it may. But pointing a rifle at a man like Vance, or anyone his age for that matter, well, I should have been locked up and sectioned off a long time ago in that case. That's all I can say about this particular debate. You have the footage showing the whole of that visit. Journalists were there. And it's crystal clear for everyone to see that I wasn't even carrying a rifle during that visit. During Vance's visit, I had no need for a rifle. Any further comments would be superfluous.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can I take it, then, that on the occasion you weren't carrying a rifle, let alone pointing a rifle at Mr. Vance or in his general direction?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think this is a good time for us to wrap up for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll resume tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 27th day of October, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.43 p.m.,
